title: The Desert Land That No Country Claims
tags: bir tawil, borders, egypt, sudan, geography
script: Between Egypt and Sudan lies nearly eight hundred square miles of desert that neither country claims. It's called Bir Tawil. Egypt follows an 1899 border, which puts it in Sudan. Sudan follows a 1902 border, which puts it in Egypt. Why the standoff? Each line also decides who gets the Halaib Triangle, a larger area next door on the Red Sea. Claiming Bir Tawil means giving up Halaib. So nobody does.

title: Fortune Cookies Probably Came From Japan
tags: fortune cookies, food history, japan, myth busting
script: Fortune cookies aren't from China. In fact, they're hard to find there. Researchers trace them to Japan, where bakeries near Kyoto shrines still make a similar cracker with a fortune tucked into its fold. Japanese immigrants likely brought the idea to California in the early 1900s. Around World War Two, as Japanese Americans were forced into internment camps, Chinese American bakers took over production. Your fortune has a hidden past.

title: China's First Emperor Ordered a Hunt for Immortality
tags: qin shi huang, ancient china, elixir of life, emperors
script: China's first emperor ordered his entire empire to find the secret to living forever. Qin Shi Huang sent the alchemist Xu Fu across the sea to find immortals on a magical mountain. Xu Fu sailed twice, and the second time, he never came back. Wooden records found in a well in 2002 show the emperor also ordered officials everywhere to search. One region suggested a local herb. Qin Shi Huang died in 210 BC, aged forty-nine.

title: 25 People Vanished From This Ship in the Pacific
tags: mv joyita, ghost ship, pacific, unsolved
script: In 1955, a ship carrying 25 people was found drifting in the Pacific with nobody aboard. The MV Joyita had left Samoa on October 3 for a short trip to the Tokelau Islands. More than five weeks later, a passing ship spotted her half sunk, listing, and hundreds of miles off course. The life rafts were gone. So was about four tons of cargo. Her cork-lined hull had kept her afloat. An official inquiry called it inexplicable.

title: The Bird That Can Sound Like a Chainsaw
tags: lyrebird, birds, australia, mimicry
script: Deep in Australia's forests lives a bird that can sound like a chainsaw. The lyrebird builds its song from sounds around it, imitating at least twenty other bird species. But some go much further. Lyrebirds have been filmed mimicking car alarms, camera shutters, and power tools. One captive bird at Adelaide Zoo picked up construction noises while a nearby enclosure was being built. So if you hear a chainsaw in the rainforest, check the trees first.

title: The Night Los Angeles Fought an Invisible Enemy
tags: battle of los angeles, 1942, world war two, false alarm, california
script: In February 1942, Los Angeles fought a battle against nothing. Just months after Pearl Harbor, radar picked up something approaching the coast. Sirens wailed, the city went dark, and anti-aircraft guns fired more than fourteen hundred shells into the night sky. Searchlights swept the clouds. But no enemy planes were ever found. The Navy Secretary called it a false alarm caused by jittery nerves. The likely culprit? A stray weather balloon.

title: Two Islands 2.4 Miles Apart, but 21 Hours Apart
tags: diomede islands, date line, bering strait, alaska, russia
script: These two islands sit just 2.4 miles apart, but their clocks are about twenty-one hours apart. In the Bering Strait, Little Diomede belongs to the United States. Big Diomede belongs to Russia. The International Date Line runs between them, so Big Diomede is nicknamed Tomorrow Island, and Little Diomede, Yesterday Isle. In winter, sea ice can bridge the gap, but crossing isn't allowed. From yesterday, you can see tomorrow.

title: The Earl Behind the Sandwich Story May Be Fiction
tags: sandwich, food history, earl of sandwich, myth busting
script: The sandwich really is named after an earl. But the famous story may be made up. Legend says John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, gambled for twenty four hours straight and asked for meat between bread so he never had to leave the card table. That tale comes from a 1772 French travel book. His biographer thinks he more likely ate it at his desk, buried in work. Either way, his title became lunch.

title: Sparta's One-Word Reply to a Conqueror
tags: sparta, ancient greece, laconic, philip of macedon
script: One of history's greatest comebacks was a single word. Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, was conquering Greece. According to the ancient writer Plutarch, he sent the Spartans a threat: if I invade Laconia, I will drive you out. The Spartans wrote back: if. Philip did later invade. But Sparta's homeland, Laconia, was so famous for this kind of short, sharp talk that it gave English a word. Laconic.

title: Glenn Miller Took Off and Was Never Seen Again
tags: glenn miller, world war ii, disappearance, music history
script: One of America's most famous bandleaders boarded a small plane in England and was never seen again. On December 15, 1944, Major Glenn Miller took off from an airfield near Bedford, bound for France. He was heading there to arrange a Christmas broadcast for the troops. The single-engine Norseman flew out over the English Channel and simply vanished. No wreckage has ever been found. Bad weather? Mechanical failure? The music lived on. The answer didn't.

title: Crows Held a Grudge Against One Face for Years
tags: crows, birds, animal intelligence, memory
script: Crows can remember your face, and hold a grudge for years. In 2006, a University of Washington professor trapped seven crows while wearing a scary mask, then released them. Afterward, anyone wearing that mask on campus got scolded by angry, squawking crows. Even crows that were never caught joined in, and passed it on to their young. People in a neutral Dick Cheney mask were ignored. The scolding peaked in 2013. Seventeen years later, it finally faded.

title: The 1876 Plot to Steal Lincoln's Body
tags: abraham lincoln, 1876, secret service, counterfeiters, us history
script: In 1876, criminals tried to kidnap Abraham Lincoln, eleven years after he died. A gang of counterfeiters planned to take his coffin from its tomb in Springfield. Their ransom: two hundred thousand dollars, plus the release of their jailed star engraver. But one member of the gang was a Secret Service informant. Agents waited at the tomb, and the plotters were soon arrested. Illinois had no grave-robbing law, so they were charged with trying to steal a coffin.

title: The Most Remote Inhabited Island on Earth
tags: tristan da cunha, remote islands, south atlantic, geography
script: Its nearest inhabited neighbor is about fifteen hundred miles away. Tristan da Cunha, in the South Atlantic, is considered the most remote inhabited island on Earth. There's no airport. Ships from Cape Town take about a week. Around two hundred and twenty people live in one settlement, called Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. In 1961, a volcano forced everyone to evacuate to England. Two years later, most of them came home.

title: A Bug Collector Pushed for Daylight Saving Time
tags: daylight saving time, new zealand, insects, odd origins
script: Daylight saving time was championed by a bug collector. In 1895, New Zealand entomologist George Vernon Hudson presented a paper proposing a seasonal shift of the clocks. He worked shifts at the Wellington post office, and he valued every hour of evening light for hunting insects. Several members of the society ridiculed the idea. Today, clocks across much of the world spring forward and fall back. Thank a moth enthusiast.

title: The Philosopher Who Told Alexander to Move
tags: diogenes, alexander the great, ancient greece, philosophy
script: The most powerful man in the world once got told to step aside. Alexander the Great visited the philosopher Diogenes, who reportedly slept in a large clay jar in Athens. Alexander found him relaxing in the sun in Corinth and asked if he wanted anything. Diogenes replied: yes, stand a little out of my sun. According to Plutarch, Alexander admired him anyway, saying: if I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes.

title: The Explorer Who Vanished Hunting a Lost City
tags: percy fawcett, amazon, lost city of z, explorers
script: In 1925, a British explorer walked into the Amazon to find a lost city and never walked out. Percy Fawcett called his city Z. He set off into Brazil's Mato Grosso with his son Jack and a young friend. His last letter warned they would disappear from civilization for a while. Then, nothing. Theories range from getting lost to deadly conflict. The twist? Researchers later found traces of large ancient settlements in that region. He wasn't entirely wrong.

title: Astronauts Come Home Taller. It Doesn't Last.
tags: astronauts, space, human body, nasa
script: Astronauts can come back from space a little taller. On Earth, gravity is constantly squeezing your spine. In microgravity, that pressure disappears, and the vertebrae can relax and expand. NASA scientists say astronauts can grow up to three percent taller. For a six-foot person, that's about two extra inches. NASA even used ultrasound on the space station to study it. The catch? Back on Earth, gravity wins, and the extra height disappears within a few months.

title: Two Founding Fathers Died on the Same July 4th
tags: john adams, thomas jefferson, july 4, 1826, founding fathers
script: Two American founders died on the same day, and it was the Fourth of July. On July 4, 1826, exactly fifty years after the Declaration of Independence was adopted, Thomas Jefferson died at Monticello. About five hours later, John Adams died too. Once bitter rivals, they had become pen pals in old age. Adams's last words were reportedly, 'Thomas Jefferson still survives.' He never knew his old friend was already gone.

title: This 4,500-Year-Old City Had Covered Drains
tags: mohenjo-daro, indus valley, pakistan, ancient cities, archaeology
script: Around 2500 BC, one city already had planned streets and covered drains. Mohenjo-daro, in today's Pakistan, was one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, laid out on a grid and built mostly of fired brick. It had hundreds of wells and a waterproofed public pool known as the Great Bath. It was abandoned around 1700 BC. And its writing still hasn't been deciphered. A brilliant city, and we can't read a word.

title: The Man Who Declared Himself Emperor of the US
tags: emperor norton, san francisco, eccentrics, 1800s
script: In 1859, a San Francisco man declared himself Emperor of the United States, and the city played along. Joshua Norton sent his proclamation to a newspaper, which printed it. He wore a military coat with gold epaulets and issued royal decrees, including one abolishing Congress. He called for a bridge across the bay to Oakland. Some restaurants accepted his homemade money. When he died in 1880, around ten thousand people came to say goodbye.

title: Pythagoras Had a Strange Rule About Beans
tags: pythagoras, ancient greece, philosophy, beans
script: The man behind your geometry homework had a serious problem with beans. Pythagoras, the ancient Greek thinker, reportedly banned his followers from eating fava beans. Why? Nobody knows for sure. Ancient writers suggested beans were linked to souls and the afterlife. Modern researchers have wondered about favism, a reaction some people have to the beans. One legend even claims Pythagoras refused to escape through a bean field. Historians doubt it, but the bean ban was real enough.

title: When Agatha Christie Became a Real Mystery
tags: agatha christie, disappearance, 1920s, authors
script: In 1926, a rising mystery writer became the subject of a real one. On December 3, Agatha Christie left her home, and her car was found abandoned the next morning. Over a thousand police and thousands of volunteers searched the countryside. Eleven days later, she turned up at a hotel in Harrogate, registered under the surname of the woman her husband was seeing. Doctors said memory loss. Critics said publicity stunt. Her autobiography never mentions it.

title: A Sloth's Fur Is a Whole Tiny Ecosystem
tags: sloths, rainforest, animals, nature
script: A sloth's fur is a tiny living ecosystem. Green algae grows in its shaggy coat, alongside beetles, fungi, bacteria, and special sloth moths. In 2014, scientists studying sloths in Costa Rica found that the moths help bring in nutrients that feed the algae. And that algae turned up in sloth stomachs. Sloths may be snacking on their own fur garden for extra energy. It might even help them hide from harpy eagles. Lazy? More like self-sufficient.

title: The Fairy Photos That Fooled Sherlock's Creator
tags: cottingley fairies, arthur conan doyle, hoax, 1917, photography
script: In 1917, two English cousins photographed fairies. Elsie was sixteen. Frances was nine. Their pictures from the village of Cottingley showed tiny winged figures right beside them. In 1920, Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of logical detective Sherlock Holmes, published the photos as genuine in The Strand Magazine. Decades later, in 1983, the cousins admitted the fairies were paper cutouts. Yet Frances insisted one photo was real until the end.

title: Rome's Ancient Dome Still Holds a World Record
tags: pantheon, rome, roman engineering, concrete, architecture
script: Nearly nineteen hundred years after it was finished, this Roman dome still holds a world record. The Pantheon's dome spans about 142 feet, and it's still the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth. There's no steel inside. The builders used lighter material, like pumice, toward the top. At the center is a twenty-seven-foot opening called the oculus, open to the sky. Rain falls right inside. And it still hosts Mass today.

title: The Luckiest Fool Who Sold Coal to Newcastle
tags: timothy dexter, eccentrics, business, 1700s
script: Timothy Dexter may have been the luckiest fool in American history. Rivals reportedly urged him to ship bed warming pans to the tropical West Indies. They were sold as molasses ladles. He reportedly shipped coal to Newcastle, England, a coal town. It arrived during a miners' strike. Then he wrote a book with no punctuation. When readers complained, he added a page of punctuation marks and told them to sprinkle them wherever they pleased.

title: Romans Didn't Have Rooms for Vomiting
tags: ancient rome, vomitorium, myths, latin
script: Romans did not have special rooms for throwing up during feasts. A vomitorium was actually an exit. The word appears in the writer Macrobius, describing the passages that let crowds pour in and out of theaters and amphitheaters, as if the building were spewing people out. No ancient source ever used it for a room to be sick in. That gross idea took hold in the 1800s and was popularized by novelists. The vomitorium was a doorway.

title: The Film Pioneer Who Vanished From a Train
tags: louis le prince, film history, disappearance, inventors
script: The man who may have filmed the first moving pictures stepped onto a train and disappeared. In 1888, Louis Le Prince filmed a few seconds of people walking in a garden in Leeds, England. It's among the oldest surviving film footage. In September 1890, his brother saw him off at the station in Dijon, France. He was bound for Paris, then America, to show his invention. He never arrived. Years later, Thomas Edison got the credit.

title: This Small Bird Sees Two Summers Every Year
tags: arctic tern, birds, migration, animals
script: This bird weighs about as much as a bar of soap, yet it makes the longest known migration of any bird. The Arctic tern breeds in the Arctic, then flies to Antarctica and back. Tracking showed some terns cover about seventy thousand kilometers a year, zigzagging to ride the winds. Chasing summer at both ends of Earth, it sees more daylight than any other creature. Over a lifetime, that's like flying to the Moon and back three times.

title: The Theft That Made the Mona Lisa Famous
tags: mona lisa, louvre, art theft, 1911, picasso
script: The Mona Lisa became the world's most famous painting partly because someone stole it. On August 21, 1911, it vanished from the Louvre in Paris. Police questioned the poet Guillaume Apollinaire, and even Pablo Picasso. Both were innocent. The real thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, who had once worked at the Louvre. The painting stayed missing for over two years, until he tried to sell it in Florence. By then, everyone knew her face.
